venues.name: The Local
venues.shortDescription: Neighborhood bar and restaurant known for showcasing some of Nashville's best local artists. With live music every night, it's a go-to spot for writer's rounds, artist showcases, and discovering new talent.
venues.whatToExpect: Dining tables wrap around a small center stage in a dimly lit room that feels more like a neighborhood restaurant than bar. It's a casual, no dress code, come as you are type of vibe. You can grab a beer on tap, can, or a stiffly poured mixed drink. The food is way better than any bar menu has a right to be. The wraps and club sandwich are solid, but make sure you grab the thick-cut fries. The stage is small but it stays busy, with live music running every night of the week. On any weeknight, a country star like Riley Green, Jamey Johnson, or Zac Brown might drop in for a few songs. When they're not on stage, you might just catch some local legends enjoying a beer and taking in the music themselves.

venues.name: The Station Inn
venues.shortDescription: Legendary listening room known for hosting some of the best bluegrass and roots music in the world. An intimate venue where you can experience Nashville's best showcase of bluegrass up close.
venues.whatToExpect: If you blink, you might miss this legendary venue that's almost hidden between high-end dining options and boujee rooftop hotel bars. For roughly 50 years, The Station Inn has been keeping bluegrass, classic country, and roots music alive in Nashville. Walking through the front door feels like stepping back in time as you'll be greeted at the door by a sweet southern staff collecting the cash-only cover. From there, you'll grab your seat on a first come first serve basis at a chair, table, or a salvaged seat from a tour bus along the back wall. You can grab a beer or soft drink from the bar and order some ballpark style food like pizza, nachos, or popcorn. This single story room puts you nearly eye-level with the stage with no bad angles in sight. You'll feel like you're part of the performance in this intimate honky-tonk dive. Country and bluegrass icons like Bill Monroe, John Prine, Ricky Skaggs, Dolly Parton, Vince Gill, and rising stars alike have taken the stage or watched from the crowd.

venues.name: Live Oak
venues.shortDescription: Local bar and restaurant featuring live music from emerging and established Nashville artists. A laid-back spot for catching songwriter rounds and casual country performances throughout the week.

venues.name: The Listening Room Cafe
venues.shortDescription: A premier listening room known for hosting songwriter rounds with some of Nashville's top writers. A seated, intimate setting focused on storytelling and acoustic performances.
venues.whatToExpect: The Listening Room operates out of a historic International Harvester building on 4th Ave South, where Johnny Cash once built his infamous tractor. The main room holds 255 seated guests and runs two shows every night, built around songwriter rounds where artists perform their own original material and share the stories behind the songs. The writers behind some of the biggest names in modern country music play this stage regularly, with Morgan Wallen, Luke Combs, and Lainey Wilson all represented. Chris Stapleton, Carly Pearce, and HARDY have all made appearances of their own. The food leans Southern bar with a few standouts worth ordering: the smoked wings are finished with a flash fry and come in a healthy range of sauces, and the Yazoo Taco Chili is made with locally brewed Yazoo beer. Craft cocktails, beer, and wine round out the bar. Most shows carry a cover charge between $5 and $15, plus a $15 per person food and drink minimum at a main room table. The venue claims the best sound system in Nashville and the layout gives every seat a clear view of the stage. If you're not ready to commit to a full show, the front bar runs free live music daily during happy hour from 4 to 5:30pm. Valet parking is $15, paid nightly.

venues.name: The Bluebird Cafe
venues.shortDescription: World-famous Nashville listening room known for its intimate songwriter rounds featuring some of the industry's top writers. A bucket-list experience where the focus stays on the music and the stories behind it.
venues.whatToExpect: The Bluebird Cafe sits in a small Green Hills strip mall about 20 minutes from downtown, with almost no signage from the street. The room holds around 90 people at small candlelit tables. It doesn't look like much from the outside, and that's part of what makes it one of the most storied rooms in country music. The signature format is "in the round," four songwriters seated in the center of the room, taking turns playing their own songs and telling the stories behind them. You might not recognize the names on any given night, but the writers in that room are behind some of the biggest songs in country music. Garth Brooks played an open mic here in 1987 and walked out with a Capitol Records deal. Scott Borchetta saw a 15-year-old Taylor Swift perform here in 2004 and signed her to what became Big Machine. The quiet policy is real; conversation during performances is discouraged and the crowd self-polices. Tickets go on sale Monday mornings and sell out in minutes, sometimes seconds, so have the website open before they drop. There's a $15 food and drink minimum per person at most shows. Parking is limited: the small lot out front fills fast, and parking in the wrong strip mall spot will get you towed. The gravel lot behind the building, accessed via the alley on Hillsboro Pike, is the better option.

venues.name: Bourbon Street Blues and Boogie Bar
venues.shortDescription: Lively Printer's Alley venue known for live blues and jazz music in a classic New Orleans-style setting. A go-to spot for late-night live bands, dancing, and a Mardi Gras-style atmosphere.
venues.whatToExpect: You'll hear it before you see it. The Bourbon Street Blues and Boogie Bar announces itself with a low growl of brass and guitar echoing down Printer's Alley. Once inside, the low ceilings keep the sound thick and close, you feel the music more than at most venues. The room is tight, but there's a second level with balcony seating and better sightlines. Reservations are worth making, especially on weekends, since the place fills fast. On the food and drink side, the Cajun menu is genuine: gumbo, voodoo wings, alligator bites, and the Big Easy Hurricane are the way to go. Rooted in Printer's Alley for over 25 years, thousands of musicians have played this stage, including legends like James Brown and B.B. King. In a city built on country music, there's no other room in Nashville that sounds like this.

venues.name: The Nashville Palace
venues.shortDescription: Classic country honky tonk near the Grand Ole Opry featuring live bands and a traditional Nashville music atmosphere. Known for line dancing, local performers, and an authentic country music vibe.
venues.whatToExpect: Nashville Palace opened in 1977 as a place for Opry performers to unwind after their sets, and that DNA still shapes what the room feels like today. It's unpretentious in every way: walls lined with memorabilia, four bars spread throughout, two rooms: one holding the ballroom with the main wooden dance floor, and the other with the live music stage that stays busy with traditional country music. Line dancing is as much a part of the experience as the music, with free lessons Tuesday through Sunday nights starting around 7pm. After you've worked up an appetite dancing, grab some Southern comfort food like the artist favorite Smoked Bologna Sandwich, a BBQ plate, or the fried catfish sandwich along with another round. Parking is free and easy, which is rare for a Nashville music venue. Randy Travis was discovered here while working as a cook and dishwasher. George Jones was a regular. The Palace sits directly across from the Grand Ole Opry, so pairing the two makes for the perfect night out.

venues.name: Anzie Blue
venues.shortDescription: Intimate venue in Hillsboro Village known for hosting live shows and songwriter rounds. A smaller, seated space where you can catch local artists and emerging talent in a relaxed setting.
venues.whatToExpect: Anzie Blue sits across the street from the Belcourt Theatre, one of the original homes of the Grand Ole Opry, just blocks from Music Row in Hillsboro Village. It opened as a live music venue in March 2023. Nashville's only woman-owned music venue, it's co-owned by Marcie Allen Van Mol, a 30-year music industry veteran who's landed brand partnerships for the Rolling Stones, Katy Perry, and Billy Joel, and her husband Derek Van Mol. The nearly 4,000-square-foot space leans into a luxe speakeasy look, with a 28-foot marble bar and a custom-built stage, holding up to 250 people standing or 150 seated. Steve Earle, Grace Bowers, Dierks Bentley, Caitlyn Smith, and Joy Oladokun have all played there. A monthly Women of Country showcase and a recurring Drag Experience series are two of its signature ongoing programs. It's also an official AMERICANAFEST and Tin Pan South venue. A Pride Month flash mob it hosted in 2023 went viral with over 60 million views. Parking is available in an adjacent garage, with the first hour free.

venues.name: The Basement East
venues.shortDescription: Popular East Nashville concert venue known for hosting touring indie and rock acts. A go-to spot for catching live music outside the Broadway scene.
venues.whatToExpect: The Basement East, locally known as The Beast, is a dark, warehouse-style room with a raised stage and mostly standing room up front. Limited tables and chairs are available but go fast on a first-come-first-served basis, so arriving early is the move. There's a small mezzanine above the main floor for better sightlines if you want to hang back, and a spacious outdoor deck where you can step out between sets for a view of downtown Nashville across the river. Parking is easy: Fireman's Credit Union directly across the street opens its lot to concertgoers from 6PM to 3AM. Opened in 2015, The Beast built its reputation fast by consistently booking touring acts you'd never expect in a room this size. Beck, Cage the Elephant, Brandi Carlile, Luke Combs, and John Prine have all played here. The venue rebuilt after a tornado tore through East Nashville in 2020 and hasn't slowed down since.

venues.name: 6th & Peabody
venues.shortDescription: Outdoor beer garden and distillery featuring live music, food, and a high-energy atmosphere in the heart of downtown. A go-to spot for live country music, drinks, and a little bit of everything Nashville has to offer.
venues.whatToExpect: Moonshine distillery meets outdoor beer garden meets sports bar with live music. Ole Smoky Moonshine & Whiskey tastings run daily with no need for reservations. YeeHaw Brewing offers flights as well as a palate cleanser of your choosing between moonshine samples. You can catch live music and weekly writers rounds both outside and in. If you need a bite to eat, grab some tacos or a Daddy's Dog, a late-night staple locals have been grabbing on the way home from Broadway for years. Come football season, this is the place to be especially if you're a Vols fan. Locals will be cheering on Rocky Top on the big screen.

venues.name: Exit/In
venues.shortDescription: Historic Nashville concert venue known for hosting touring rock and indie acts. A staple of the local music scene with a long legacy of artists passing through its stage.
venues.whatToExpect: Exit/In has been at the same address on Elliston Place since 1971, which puts it among the oldest continuously operating rock clubs in the country. The room is mostly standing, dark, and intimate at around 500 capacity, with a small first-come-first-served mezzanine upstairs for better sightlines. The Wall of Fame above the bar is worth the read: over 250 hand-painted name plates of artists who've sold out the room, from The Ramones and The Police to Johnny Cash and Muddy Waters. Jimmy Buffett played his first Nashville show here. Steve Martin once took the entire audience out for burgers mid-show. The venue appeared in Robert Altman's 1975 film Nashville. Exit/In is now an official Nashville Historical Landmark, and the booking still reflects it. The venue is card-only, no cash. Parking on Elliston Place is tight; the pay lot on Louise Avenue behind the venue is the most reliable option.

venues.name: The Basement
venues.shortDescription: Small, intimate concert venue known for showcasing emerging artists and up-and-coming touring acts. A go-to spot for discovering new music in a close, high-energy setting.

venues.name: The End
venues.shortDescription: Small, divey rock venue known for hosting local bands and touring indie and punk acts. A longtime staple of Nashville's rock scene with a raw, high-energy atmosphere.
venues.whatToExpect: The End sits at 2219 Elliston Place, on a stretch locals call the Rock Block. The space started as Amy's, a dive bar and pool hall, before becoming a venue called Elliston Square. Bruce Fitzpatrick had been booking Nashville clubs since around 1980, helping launch early local shows for R.E.M. and Jason and the Scorchers. He later spent years booking the legendary Exit/In, just down the block, before reopening this space as The End in 1999. The room holds around 200. It's a divey space, exposed brick covered in old show posters and low light. The list of bands who've played this room reads like a punk and indie history lesson: The Flaming Lips, Minor Threat, The White Stripes, R.E.M., Fugazi, Mastodon, The Black Crowes, Sleater-Kinney, and Ty Segall have all played here. It's an events-based venue rather than a walk-in bar, open only on nights something's booked. Shows run 18+, with a typical $5 cover and doors opening around 9pm. Parking is street-only around Elliston Place, including Hayes Street behind the venue and Louise Avenue beside it.

venues.name: Marathon Music Works
venues.shortDescription: Mid-size concert venue known for hosting touring artists in a spacious, industrial-style setting. A go-to spot for live shows that feel bigger than a club but still up close.
venues.whatToExpect: Marathon Music Works occupies an early-1900s auto plant, once home to Marathon Motor Works, the first fully functional car manufacturer in the South. That title stood until General Motors opened its Saturn plant in Spring Hill, Tennessee, in 1990. When it reopened in November 2011, the venue took its name from that history through a community naming contest. The room holds 1,500 standing across 14,000 square feet of exposed brick, steel beams, and polished concrete. Bookings swing wide, with recent and upcoming acts ranging from Poppy and the Sex Pistols' surviving members to Thundercat and Isaiah Rashad. The venue is cashless. Doors run first come, first served, so arriving early gets you closer to the stage, not just a spot in line. Most of the venue is open to all ages depending on the show, but a separate craft cocktail bar, William Collier's, requires 21+ to enter. Three more bars are split between the main floor and an upstairs loft. Daddy's Dogs handles the food. Parking is limited, so ridesharing is the strong recommendation, with a designated pickup spot near the entrance.

venues.name: 3rd & Lindsley
venues.shortDescription: Established live music venue known for hosting songwriter rounds and Americana-focused performances. A seated, music-first setting built for hearing the stories behind the songs.

venues.name: Santa's Pub
venues.shortDescription: Christmas-themed double-wide dive bar known for some of the rowdiest karaoke in Nashville. A cash-only local favorite where you can sing your heart out and experience a piece of old Nashville.
venues.whatToExpect: Picture a Christmas-themed double-wide trailer where rowdy karaoke makes locals and tourists alike the stars of the show; that's Santa's Pub. This legendary, cash-only dive bar is the ultimate Off Broadway spot to grab the mic while enjoying cheap, cold beer or seltzers (no liquor in sight). A night out at Santa's is like experiencing a slice of old Nashville before the artist-backed honky-tonks drew all the tourist attention. The late owner Edwin Denzel "Santa" Irwin established an "all are welcome," family-like atmosphere that continues to live on today. And yes, he looked exactly like Santa Claus. The environment he created has brought music superstars from Ed Sheeran to Kelsea Ballerini to Kid Rock through the door to sing a late-night set with locals. You never know when one might show up next.

venues.name: Losers Bar & Grill
venues.shortDescription: Divey Midtown honky tonk known for live country music and a mix of locals, industry regulars, and late-night crowds. A go-to spot for drinks, live bands, and never quite knowing who you'll run into.
venues.whatToExpect: Losers opened in 2005 as a hangout for Nashville's music industry crowd, a place for songwriters and industry folks to talk shop and hear live music off Broadway. The vibe is dive bar all the way: neon signs, two stages (one inside and a small one on the enclosed first-floor deck with garage doors), respectably priced drinks and bar food, and a crowd that mixes industry regulars, locals, and tourists. Head upstairs to an open-air rooftop deck with big screens and a full view of the Midtown skyline. Live music runs seven nights a week, with Losers Live full band showcase running Monday nights at 8pm, featuring live original music. During the summer, Losers Live takes it outdoors for their parking lot concert series. It's basically a free first-come, first-served block party with a multi-artist showcase of rising songwriters and major hitmakers. Recent outdoor acts include Jon Pardi, Chase Rice, and Riley Green with past acts as big as Morgan Wallen. The venue connects directly to Riley Green's Duck Blind next door, so you can check it out without ever actually leaving. Some free parking is available in the area, which is rare for Midtown Nashville. Celebrity bartender nights bring country artists behind the bar a few times a year. On any given night, the person next to you at the bar might be someone you've heard on the radio.

venues.name: Riley Green's Duck Blind
venues.shortDescription: Casual Midtown bar known for live country music and plenty of TVs. A go-to spot for catching the game, live bands, and the occasional country artist drop-in.
venues.whatToExpect: Duck Blind took over the old Winners Bar and Grill spot on Division Street, and Riley Green's connection to the place goes back long before his name was on the sign. He played some of his earliest Nashville shows here, made key industry connections within its walls, and when the space became available, he jumped at it. They kept the original stage and preserved the bar top that still reads "WINNERS" underneath the new branding. TVs are everywhere and easy to see from most seats, making it a natural game day spot. The drink list runs bottles and cans with a full bar, no draft beer. The menu has a few Riley's Choice items worth ordering: the Duck Fries and BBQ Chicken Wrap are the go-tos. Wednesday nights are for the Cold Beer Country Showcase, a weekly live music event featuring rising and local artists performing original sets starting at 8:30PM. Show up on any given night and there's a real chance Riley Green walks in, jumps behind the bar to mix drinks, or ends up on stage with whoever's playing. Post Malone has been caught doing the same.

venues.name: Commodore Grill
venues.shortDescription: Casual restaurant and bar known for hosting live country music and songwriter rounds. A laid-back spot where you can grab a meal and catch local artists throughout the week.

venues.name: Nashville Municipal Auditorium
venues.shortDescription: Large indoor venue known for hosting concerts, events, and touring acts across a variety of genres. A flexible space that regularly brings bigger performances to downtown Nashville.

venues.name: Ascend Amphitheater
venues.shortDescription: Outdoor amphitheater located along the river, known for hosting touring artists and larger live shows. A go-to spot for concerts with city skyline views and a more open, scenic setting.
venues.whatToExpect: Ascend sits along the Cumberland River at the edge of downtown Nashville. The Broadway corridor and city skyline rise directly behind the stage, and on a clear evening with the sun going down, that backdrop is hard to find anywhere else in the city. Outside of the views, it's a solid outdoor amphitheater with reserved seating up front and a large sloped GA lawn behind it. A blanket or chair is an option for the lawn but not a requirement. Sound carries well across the entire space and the video screens keep you locked in no matter where you land. Rideshare is the move on show nights since downtown parking is expensive and unpredictable. Ascend has won Pollstar's outdoor venue award more than once since opening in 2015 and books big touring acts across a range of genres. Broadway is steps away when the show ends, SoBro venues are close, and East Nashville is a short rideshare if you want to keep the night going somewhere with a little more local feel.

venues.name: Scoreboard Bar & Grill
venues.shortDescription: Music Valley bar and restaurant known for live country music and a steady mix of locals and visitors. A casual spot for drinks, live bands, and a classic Nashville bar experience near the Opry.
venues.whatToExpect: Scoreboard opened on July 9, 1996, named after the section of the newspaper sports page where box scores and betting lines used to run. Nearly 30 years later, it's still under the same ownership, which the venue claims makes it the longest-running, same-owner licensed beer establishment in Nashville. The place is built for watching games: 75-plus TVs, pool tables, a Golden Tee machine, official backer-bar status for the Green Bay Packers and the Nashville Predators, plus a regular home for LSU football watch parties. Seating splits between an indoor bar and a covered outdoor deck. Live music runs daily alongside live sports. The hot chicken runs a named heat scale from "Sissy" up to "Hiroshima," a specialty strong enough to land the place a spot on Food Network. The rest of the menu leans on hickory-smoked meats, pulled pork, brisket, ribs, done in house, and a rotating list of 10+ Bushwacker flavors at the bar. Every Saturday starting in March, an all-you-can-eat crawfish, shrimp, and oyster boil runs from noon to 5pm, with live music picking back up later that evening.

venues.name: Tennessee Brew Works
venues.shortDescription: Local brewery and restaurant known for hosting live acoustic sets and songwriter-style performances. A laid-back spot to grab a beer, enjoy the food, and catch live music throughout the week.

venues.name: The Pinnacle
venues.shortDescription: Downtown concert venue at Nashville Yards known for touring artists, comedy, and larger live events. A state-of-the-art space built for big shows with strong sound, lighting, and production.
venues.whatToExpect: The Pinnacle opened at Nashville Yards in February 2025, filling a real gap in the city's concert lineup. It's a bigger, more modern room than the Ryman, but nowhere near the scale of Bridgestone Arena, sitting comfortably in between at a 4,500 capacity across 88,000 square feet. The horseshoe balcony wraps the entire floor in a U-shape, with rail-side standing, seated sections, and a first-come, first-served bleacher area for a more relaxed way to watch. The general admission floor below has tiered risers in the back, so you're not stuck standing elbow-to-elbow with the crowd, and some shows offer seated floor tickets instead of standing GA entirely. Between the two levels, there's not a bad view in the house. Seven cashless bars are spread across the venue, and bathrooms are evenly spaced too, keeping lines short during sold-out shows. The building doubles as a gallery of sorts, with murals from 20+ local Nashville artists covering the concourses and walls. It's an all-ages, fully ADA-compliant space with elevators on every level. Rideshare is the easiest way in and out, with drop-off right at 9th Ave N and Commerce St. The box office runs Tuesday through Saturday, 10am to 6pm, and opens two hours before doors on show nights.

venues.name: Brooklyn Bowl
venues.shortDescription: Multi-purpose venue known for hosting touring artists across a range of genres alongside bowling, food, and drinks. A go-to spot for live shows in a lively, all-in-one setting.
venues.whatToExpect: Brooklyn Bowl is built to be your entire night out. The space combines a full concert venue, 19 bowling lanes, a full-service restaurant, four bars, and a rooftop patio with views of the Nashville Sounds stadium, First Horizon Park. You never need to leave for food or drinks, and you never miss a second of the show. Bowl a frame, turn around, and the stage is right there. If bowling isn't your thing, the venue holds up to 1,200 across a standing room GA floor and a balcony above. The food comes from Blue Ribbon, their award-winning restaurant group out of New York. Skip the basics and go for the French bread pizzas or the Rock. And. Roll. Fries, which are essentially cajun poutine. The venue is cashless and most shows run 18+ or 21+, with all-ages nights listed on the calendar. There's no dedicated parking lot. A few free street spots in Germantown are worth hunting for, but paid lots within walking distance are the more reliable option. Brooklyn Bowl has won Billboard's top Central U.S. club or theater award and books across rock, indie, soul, and beyond.

venues.name: Star Rover Sound
venues.shortDescription: Restaurant and live music venue known for country and roots-focused performances in a unique, retro-inspired setting. A sit-down experience that blends dinner and live music in a more intimate space.
venues.whatToExpect: Star Rover Sound is a steakhouse built to feel like a 1970s Nashville recording studio, with live music included most nights. It shares a building with The Optimist and Le Loup, both from the same restaurant group under chef Ford Fry. It opened in late 2022 as an elevated taqueria before pivoting to a pick-a-cut steak-forward menu: chopped steak, filet, ribeye, skirt steak, T-bone, or a double-cut chicken breast. Dessert stays simple: three pies (chocolate chess, coconut cream, apple) and soft-serve, which regulars call "Fryce Cream" when it lands on a plate of crispy fries. The booking runs wide across jazz, bluegrass, country, and Americana. One rotating set, the Imperial Blues Hour, pulls in well-known Nashville session players for a loose, jam-heavy night. Unlike most honky-tonks, the room is built quiet enough to actually hold a conversation during a set. Dinner and music run together Wednesday through Saturday from 5 to 10pm, and Sunday from 5 to 9pm, with reservations through OpenTable. If you're feeling bold, the 76er Challenge dares you to finish a 76-ounce standing rib roast with a milk roll, side salad, fries, and onion rings, all in under an hour. Finishing it gets you the meal free, a spot on the Steak Challenge wall, and a T-shirt to prove it.

venues.name: Rudy's Jazz Room
venues.shortDescription: Dedicated jazz club known for hosting live performances from local and touring musicians. An intimate, seated setting focused on high-quality jazz in the Gulch.
venues.whatToExpect: Rudy's is down a side street in The Gulch at 809 Gleaves Street. Step inside and you'll see Persian rugs on the floor, armchairs and low tables, Moroccan lights overhead, photos of jazz greats on the walls, and a Steinway Model B grand piano up front. The 50-seat room was acoustically designed so there are no dead spots and no obstructed sightlines, meaning there's not a bad seat in the house. Multiple shows run on most nights: solo piano earlier in the evening, a full combo later. Cover charges typically run $12-$24 depending on the show. Every Thursday, the room shifts into Hot Club Gypsy Jazz, a weekly night dedicated to the swing style of Django Reinhardt and Stephane Grappelli. The menu is New Orleans-inspired: gumbo, crawfish grilled cheese, and beignets are the standouts. Cocktails lean toward prohibition era classics, with local brews rounding out the bar. Rudy's is named for Rudy Wooten of the legendary Wooten Brothers family, and the Wootens perform here regularly. Tuesday is the one night they're dark. The rest of the week, this is the most serious jazz room Nashville has. Downbeat Magazine agreed, naming it among the best in the country in 2020.

venues.name: Analog
venues.shortDescription: Intimate live music venue known for hosting a mix of genres including songwriter rounds, jazz, and touring acts. A seated setting focused on the music in a more refined, lounge-style environment.

venues.name: Big Machine Distillery & Tavern
venues.shortDescription: Berry Hill distillery and tavern known for Southern food, handcrafted cocktails, and weekend live music. A casual spot for brunch, drinks, and catching acoustic sets just outside the downtown core.
venues.whatToExpect: Big Machine Distillery & Tavern is tucked into Berry Hill, a small city of its own just south of downtown. Its streets are lined with 1940s cottages that house more than 40 recording studios, along with fences painted with murals of music legends like Dolly Parton and Willie Nelson. This is the distillery's Berry Hill outpost, sister to a downtown location that runs tours and tastings. Here, the focus shifts to a full Southern brunch and dinner menu instead. Weekend mornings are the main event: brunch runs seven days a week, but Saturday and Sunday pair it with live music from 9am to 3pm, alongside bottomless Vimosas, a vodka-based mimosa made with their own Big Machine Vodka. Thursdays split the difference, trivia on the first and third week of the month, and a songwriter round called Tavern Session on the second and fourth. The menu leans into Nashville hot chicken in nearly every form: on biscuits, between waffles, piled on salads, even fried and tossed on shrimp. There's a dog-friendly patio out front and a barrel-lined back room for smaller groups or private gatherings. It's been an OpenTable Diner's Choice winner four years running, so reservations are worth making, though walk-ins are welcome too.

venues.name: City Winery
venues.shortDescription: Concert venue, restaurant, and winery known for intimate shows, comedy, food, and wine. A seated experience where live music feels more like dinner and a show than a typical night out.
venues.whatToExpect: At City Winery, dinner and a show are one and the same. The main concert room holds around 300 people, all seated, with table service running through the performance. The wine program is central: they make wine on site, which makes City Winery Nashville's only downtown winery. The food is elevated enough to be the main event on its own, Southern-inspired with Mediterranean leanings, and the kitchen handles a sold-out show night without the quality slipping. The crowd leans toward the older and quieter side than most Nashville venues, attentive but not Bluebird-level silent. Shows start on time. The calendar runs a mix of singer-songwriter nights, comedy, and touring artists across a range of genres, so there's usually something worth checking regardless of when you're in town. An upstairs lounge with two patios has views of the downtown skyline and works well for drinks before the show. Valet parking runs $6, and there's a $5 self-park lot out front, which makes City Winery more accessible than most SoBro venues.

venues.name: The East Room
venues.shortDescription: East Nashville music and comedy venue known for up-and-coming local and touring talent. A casual spot for catching live shows, comedy nights, and a more independent side of the Nashville scene.

venues.name: The Blue Room at Third Man Records
venues.shortDescription: Intimate venue at Third Man Records known for live music, cocktails, DJs, film screenings, and special events. A one-of-a-kind Nashville spot where the experience feels tied to the city's record-making culture.
venues.whatToExpect: The Blue Room sits inside Third Man Records' Nashville headquarters, the label Jack White founded in 2001 and brought to Nashville in 2009. It's billed as the world's only live venue with direct-to-acetate recording capabilities, meaning performances here can be cut straight onto vinyl on the label's vintage lathe. Songs recorded this way become part of Third Man's Blue Series, 7-inch records named after the room's signature blue hue. Billie Eilish and Finneas once recorded an intimate acoustic set there for the series. For years, the space was only open for special events, film screenings, and poetry readings. That changed in 2021, when Third Man opened it to the public three nights a week, Thursday through Saturday, 7pm to midnight. Beyond ticketed concerts, regular events include WNXP-hosted trivia nights, stand-up comedy hosted by Cortney Warner, and monthly film screenings off a 16mm projector. Most shows are general admission and standing room only. The room itself is a dreamlike, cornerless blue space, with a patio out back and a vintage dip 'n dunk photobooth. The bar serves craft cocktails and beer from Nashville breweries, along with pretzels from Fatbelly, an award-winning local bakery. It's 21 and up.

venues.name: Springwater Supper Club & Lounge
venues.shortDescription: Long-running West End bar known for live music, local bands, and a gritty Nashville feel. A classic neighborhood spot for catching shows in a casual, divey setting.
venues.whatToExpect: Springwater Supper Club & Lounge has served drinks on this same corner of West End since 1896. The building first opened as the bar for the Tennessee Centennial and International Exposition, making it older than the Parthenon replica next door. It went through Prohibition as a speakeasy, when Al Capone and Jimmy Hoffa were rumored to gamble there, spent time as a joint called the Pirate's Den, and only became Springwater in 1978. The place calls itself the oldest continuously operating bar in Tennessee, its walls lined with band stickers, dusty trophies, and random signs. Dierks Bentley once described it as a dive so rough that the stage leaked when it rained. Don't let the "supper club" name fool you. This is a small, loud, cash-only dive that leans into local punk and indie bands rather than the country you'll hear elsewhere in town. Live music runs five nights a week, Wednesday through Sunday. The Black Keys shot their "Little Black Submarines" music video on-site, turning it into a secret pop-up show for fans. Free pool and darts keep things going between sets, and both the bar and the door are cash only, though there's an ATM inside. Dogs are welcome on the front and back porches. It's 21 and up.

venues.name: The 5 Spot
venues.shortDescription: East Nashville music venue and hangout known for local bands, themed dance nights, and a steady neighborhood crowd. A go-to spot for catching the local scene in a casual, divey room away from downtown.
venues.whatToExpect: The 5 Spot opened in 2003, years before East Nashville's eclectic food scene, wine bars, and vintage shops gave the neighborhood its current pull. Todd Sherwood took over booking in 2007 in his mid-twenties, and nearly twenty years and more than 50,000 shows later, he's still the one setting the calendar. Seating is first come, first served, with doors opening 30 minutes before showtime, so arrive early if you prefer not to stand. The booking doesn't sit in one lane. Rock, country, funk, and straight songwriter sets all show up in the same week. Weekly nights have their own following: Sunday is karaoke, Monday runs a Blue Monday set into a later Motown Monday, and Tuesday pairs an early songwriter open mic with a full band set called Tight 5 Tuesday. All shows are 21 and up, and tickets typically run $5 to $10 a night.

venues.name: Love & Exile
venues.shortDescription: East Nashville winery, cocktail bar, and patio spot known for drinks, local eats, and live events. A casual neighborhood hang where wine, cocktails, and a social East Side atmosphere are as much the draw as the music.

venues.name: The Grand Ole Opry
venues.shortDescription: World-famous country music venue near Opryland known for showcasing legends, rising artists, and weekly live performances. A bucket-list Nashville experience built around the history and future of country music.
venues.whatToExpect: The Grand Ole Opry is the mecca of country music and home of the longest continuously running radio broadcast in U.S. history. A night at The Opry is a multi-artist show that features 6-8 performers ranging from legends of the genre to today's biggest stars and rising talent. Each artist plays a few songs and shares a story or two before rotating to the next performer. No two lineups are ever the same. Whether you're a diehard country music fan or just there to see what made the genre famous, the Opry has a way of winning everyone over. The Opry House is a welcoming and comfortable environment with food and drinks for purchase (yes they have booze too), cushioned pew-style seating with great views from every section, and a room that makes you feel like part of the show. There's a reason artists still consider an Opry induction one of the highest honors in country music. You'll feel it the second you walk in the room.

venues.name: The Ryman Auditorium
venues.shortDescription: Historic downtown concert hall known as the Mother Church of Country Music and the Grand Ole Opry's most famous former home. A bucket-list Nashville venue for world-class shows, incredible acoustics, and serious music history.
venues.whatToExpect: Built in 1892 as the Union Gospel Tabernacle, the Ryman was a church before it was a music hall, and you feel that when you walk in. The stained glass windows are intact, the original wooden pews are still in place, and the sound carries in a way most modern venues can't replicate. Some seats have partial obstructed views from support columns, which the ticketing system flags upfront. The Ryman was the Grand Ole Opry's home from 1943 to 1974. It's where bluegrass was born, where Johnny Cash met June Carter, and where careers were made on napkin deals backstage. Today the calendar runs well beyond country: Bob Dylan, Harry Styles, the Wu-Tang Clan, and Lizzo have all sold it out in recent years. It's been a National Historic Landmark since 2001 and a Rock and Roll Landmark since 2022. The calendar earns both. If you're not coming for a show, the self-guided tour runs daily from 9am to 4pm. You get access to the floor, the balcony, exhibits, and a recording booth where you can lay down a track on the actual Ryman stage. Parking downtown is expensive and scarce; plan on a rideshare or budget extra time for a garage.

venues.name: Bobby's Idle Hour Tavern
venues.shortDescription: Legendary Music Row watering hole known for local songwriters, musicians, and a divey Nashville tavern feel. A laid-back spot for drinks and original songs in one of the city's most historic music neighborhoods.
venues.whatToExpect: Bobby's Idle Hour has been a fixture of Music Row since Bobby Herald and his girlfriend Dianne took over the already-known dive in 1978 and added his name to the sign. They married at the bar twelve years later. The place has changed hands six times and moved locations twice since, always staying close to where it started. It closed for nearly two years after losing its lease in 2019, reopening at its current spot on 9 Music Square S in 2021 under longtime employee and regular Josh, with the help of a few partners. A giant plywood guitar marks the entrance, distinctive enough that it's been written about well beyond local coverage. Thursday is songwriter night, when working writers from up and down the Row show up to work out new songs on each other and on the crowd. There's no cover charge for live music, and the crowd is a mix of neighborhood regulars, students, and tourists who wandered off Broadway looking for something less polished. Cards are accepted now, but the old tradition of tacking a dollar bill to the wall hasn't gone anywhere. The bar is open daily from noon to 1am.

venues.name: Doc Holliday's Saloon
venues.shortDescription: Downtown honky tonk known for live country music, cold drinks, and a fun bar atmosphere. A lively spot for catching live bands without stepping directly onto Broadway.
venues.whatToExpect: Doc Holliday's sits just steps off Broadway, but plays like an old-school honky-tonk rather than the celebrity-backed bars nearby. It's named for the real Doc Holliday, the Old West gunfighter who rode with Wyatt Earp and stood in the O.K. Corral shootout. Open since 2000, it's strictly 21 and up. The room is small, maybe 15 stools at the main bar, with a spiral staircase leading up to a second level. Spinning the drink wheel by the bar is a rite of passage, and depending on where it lands, you might owe a shot, get a shot, have to buy the band a round, or, if you're feeling bold, flash them. Live music runs every night, leaning more on covers and requests than original sets, though plenty of the performers are songwriters who mix their own material in. The Bloody Mary has its own reputation, a big pour topped with cheese skewers, sausage, shrimp, onions, olives, carrots, and bacon, regularly named among the best in Nashville. Like a lot of old-school Nashville dives, the walls are covered in patron-signed dollar bills. Here, they come down every year and the money goes to charity.

venues.name: Skull's Rainbow Room
venues.shortDescription: Historic Printer's Alley lounge known for live jazz, dinner, cocktails, and a throwback Nashville atmosphere. A seated, intimate spot for music, burlesque, and a classic night out downtown.
venues.whatToExpect: Skull's is in the basement of the Southern Turf Building at 222 Printer's Alley, which means you're heading underground into a room with two-foot-thick stone walls, low lighting, live jazz, and a speakeasy feel. The original Skull's Rainbow Room opened in 1948 under David "Skull" Schulman, who ran it until his murder onsite in 1998, and the room sat empty for nearly two decades before reopening in 2014. Elvis Presley, Johnny Cash, Patsy Cline, Etta James, Bob Dylan, and Paul McCartney all performed or spent time here. The menu has earned recognition from Condé Nast. The prime rib, rack of lamb, and pork chop are the standout entrees, portions run large, and the lobster bisque and truffle mashed potatoes are worth ordering alongside. Craft cocktails run $15 and up. The burlesque show runs Thursday through Sunday starting at 11pm, with a $25 cover kicking in at 9pm on those nights. Reservations are strongly recommended; Saturday nights book out months in advance. Walk-ins are possible at the bar earlier in the evening but a real gamble after 8pm.

venues.name: The Underdog
venues.shortDescription: East Nashville neighborhood bar known for affordable drinks, a laid-back atmosphere, and live music throughout the week. A low-key spot for catching local artists in an intimate room on Gallatin Pike.

venues.name: Skinny Dennis
venues.shortDescription: East Nashville honky tonk known for country, Americana, roots music, and regular two-step nights. A casual spot for live music, line dancing, cold drinks, and a down-home feel on Gallatin Pike.
venues.whatToExpect: Skinny Dennis is named for Outlaw Country bassist Skinny Dennis Sanchez, the 6'11" upright bass player immortalized in Guy Clark's "LA Freeway." The Nashville location opened on Gallatin Pike in early 2024 as a second outpost of the original Brooklyn bar that's been running since 2013, and Nashville Scene named it the best new honky-tonk in the city almost immediately. The room is a big horseshoe bar with booths along the walls, a proper dance floor, a game room, and a backyard with an outdoor stage. Hot peanuts hit the bar the second you sit down. The dance floor is the main event on most nights, with two-step lessons every Wednesday at 7:30pm and Sunday at 7pm, both free. Live music is nightly and the booking is serious about traditional country and Americana: Chris Scruggs, Emily Nenni, Jesse Daniel, Joshua Hedley, and Kristina Murray are all regulars. Order the old fashioned on draft or the Original Willie's Frozen Coffee, served in a blue bodega cup and named after co-owner Zephaniah OHora's dog. Sully's Smoke Shack handles food on the patio. Rideshare is strongly encouraged; on-site parking is minimal.

venues.name: Sid Gold's Request Room
venues.shortDescription: East Nashville piano karaoke bar known for live accompaniment and an electric sing-along atmosphere. A fun spot for stepping up to the mic or just watching the room turn into a show.
venues.whatToExpect: Sid Gold's is Nashville's only piano karaoke bar. The front room is your standard bar; the back room is the piano lounge. Most nights bring live piano karaoke with a start time that shifts depending on the calendar. Reservations are recommended given how small the room is, but walk-ins are genuinely welcome. Parking is easier here than most of East Nashville. Beyond the nightly singing, the calendar runs its own oddball lineup. Each week, Monday brings a show-tunes open mic and Wednesday pairs a bring-your-own-vinyl hour with a burlesque set. Once a month, there's a Disney singalong and a "Bummer Night" sad-song karaoke that's a local favorite. There's also an analog photo booth on site that uses real film for a souvenir of the night out. The room's reputation as "the most supportive room in town" isn't just marketing copy. It shows up unprompted in independent reviews too, and it's the reason first-timers terrified of singing in public tend to come back.

venues.name: Wild Beaver Saloon
venues.shortDescription: Downtown karaoke bar known for late-night singing, drinks, and a rowdy party atmosphere. A casual spot for grabbing the mic and leaning into the full Nashville karaoke experience.
venues.whatToExpect: Wild Beaver Saloon opened in Indianapolis in 2006, with the Nashville location following years later. It sits a block off Broadway on Commerce Street, just far enough from the polished, celebrity-backed tourist-trap bars on the strip, but close enough to deliver the same rowdy honky-tonk energy. The design leans into a rustic mountain lodge look, mostly covered in wood and glowing neon lights with a big neon beaver sign out front marking the entrance. The mechanical bull is center stage, and there's usually a line of people waiting to give it a shot. Karaoke runs every night, self-proclaimed as the "Best Dam Karaoke" in town. Order a Beaver Bomb (basically a vodka Red Bull in shot form) from the Beaverettes for a quick jolt before you head up to the stage to sing your heart out. It's a magnet for bachelor and bachelorette parties, though the crowd pulls in college students, downtown professionals, and locals on any given night. It's 21 and up, closed Mondays, and the latest nights run until roughly 3am on Fridays and Saturdays.

venues.name: Ms. Kelli's Karaoke Bar
venues.shortDescription: Printer's Alley karaoke bar known for a huge song list, no-cover entry, and a rowdy late-night crowd. A casual spot for singing, drinking, Jell-O shots, and keeping the night going downtown.

venues.name: The Green Light Bar
venues.shortDescription: 8th Avenue bar known for songwriter rounds, open mics, and live music from local Nashville artists. A low-key spot for hearing original songs in a chill, neighborhood setting.

venues.name: The Nations Bar & Grill
venues.shortDescription: Neighborhood bar and restaurant in The Nations known for food, drinks, and live music throughout the week. A casual spot for catching country, Americana, and bluegrass-leaning performances without leaving West Nashville.
venues.whatToExpect: The Nations Bar & Grill sits on 51st Avenue North in The Nations, a fast-growing West Nashville neighborhood where old warehouses and auto shops have turned into breweries, casual eateries, and neighborhood dive bars. Inside, it leans into that same dive-bar feel, with two covered patios out back where dogs are welcome. Friday nights bring live bluegrass, often billed as the bar's own bluegrass showcase, and a band called Bluesnado takes over every second Saturday of the month. The kitchen is known for bacon-wrapped wings, a giant soft pretzel, and a veggie burger. On Fridays, they serve a bean roll, a hefty fist-thick burrito stuffed with refried beans and topped with spicy red sauce, melted cheese, sour cream, and jalapeno. The recipe traces back to the Gold Rush, the legendary Elliston Place dive bar that closed in 2019, brought over by its longtime kitchen manager, Buster Depue. As of summer 2026, the bar is temporarily paused for renovations, working on a refreshed space and an updated menu before reopening.

venues.name: The Eighth Room
venues.shortDescription: Elevated 8th Avenue lounge and live music venue known for premium cocktails, a dress-to-impress vibe, and a historic stage tied to the old Douglas Corner space. A smaller room for catching live shows in a more refined Nashville setting.
venues.whatToExpect: The Eighth Room occupies the former home of Douglas Corner Café, a songwriter listening room that helped launch Garth Brooks, Trisha Yearwood, and Blake Shelton before closing for good in 2020. Musician Jason Hollis had played the original room himself in the '90s. When he spotted the boarded-up building on a walk near his home, he and his wife Erin bought it, reopened it as The Eighth Room in 2022, and kept the original stage intact and in use. The interior leans into a different era entirely: licensed Andy Warhol prints, 1960s Italian subway tile, and 1940s lighting fixtures throughout. It's 21 and up, dress code enforced, open Tuesday through Thursday from 5 to 10pm and Friday and Saturday from 6pm to 11pm. The room holds 72 seated and up to 150 total. Weekly programming runs jazz, DJ sets, and funk and soul nights, plus Hooked, a Tuesday night show where songwriters get 60 seconds to perform their best hook in front of a panel of real industry judges, hosted by Hollis himself. Town & Country named it one of the venues shaping culture nationally, putting it in the same company as Max's Kansas City and the Viper Room.

venues.name: Tin Roof (Demonbreun)
venues.shortDescription: Demonbreun live music joint known for bands, DJs, food, and late-night crowds near Midtown and Music Row. A casual spot for catching live music, watching the game, and staying out late.

venues.name: Odie's
venues.shortDescription: Midtown neighborhood bar and entertainment venue known for live music, DJs, sports, and the feel-good spirit of Old Dominion. A casual spot for drinks, games, and catching Nashville artists in a lively setting.

venues.name: Cannery Hall
venues.shortDescription: Historic Cannery Row venue complex known for touring artists, multiple stages, and shows across a wide range of genres. A go-to spot for concerts that can range from intimate songwriter sets to bigger live events.
venues.whatToExpect: Cannery Hall's building has stood since 1883, when it started as a flour mill. It's since cycled through several lives, including a coffee mill, a food processing facility, and a restaurant named The Cannery, where the name came from. By the early 1980s, the same family running that restaurant started letting promoters book live bands there at night, and the building took on a genuinely split identity: country legends like Reba McEntire and George Strait played by day, while rock and alternative touring acts took over after dark. TNN filmed its "New Country" concert series here regularly by 1984. The Warner family bought the building in 1992. Their later partnerships with local promoters led to Mercy Lounge, Cannery Ballroom, and The High Watt opening inside, three separate venues under one roof. Today the complex runs four distinct spaces: the Mainstage holding around 1,300, a mid-size room called The Mil around 600, the smaller Row One Stage around 300, and Amaranth, a private event space upstairs. The rooms keep their industrial bones: red-brick walls, exposed ceiling beams, and original hardwood floors throughout, refreshed by a full restoration in 2024. Bands as varied as Jane's Addiction, Iggy Pop, and Lenny Kravitz have played here in more recent years. Parking is limited and paid, but the building sits close enough to both The Gulch and Lower Broadway to make walking in from either direction the easier option.

venues.name: Cross-Eyed Critters Watering Hole
venues.shortDescription: Animatronic karaoke bar inside Graduate Nashville known for sing-alongs with a robotic backup band and a bit of Dolly-inspired flair. A quirky West End spot for karaoke, drinks, and a one-of-a-kind Nashville night out.

venues.name: Lonnie's Western Room
venues.shortDescription: Long-running Printer's Alley karaoke bar known for its classic downtown feel and late-night sing-alongs. A casual spot for grabbing drinks, getting on stage, and experiencing one of Nashville's original karaoke rooms.

venues.name: Dee's Country Cocktail Lounge
venues.shortDescription: Madison neighborhood bar known for live country, roots music, classic cocktails, and a strong local following. A divey, music-first spot for catching bands outside the downtown scene.
venues.whatToExpect: Dee's Country Cocktail Lounge is housed inside a converted triple-wide trailer in Madison, a neighborhood that was once home to country and bluegrass royalty: Bill Monroe, Earl Scruggs, and Patsy Cline all lived there. Jam sessions at Scruggs' house were known to pull in bluegrass' biggest names, and Cline was part of a wave of musicians who moved to Madison once they started making real money in the industry. Owner Amy Dee opened the place in 2016 because she felt Nashville didn't have a proper classic country bar, so she built one herself. Inside, it's wood paneling, a jukebox loaded with old country records, and a 1970s dive-bar feel throughout. NPR named it one of the city's top 10 music venues, and Esquire put it on its list of the Best 27 Bars in America in 2020. Musician Margo Price has even worked the bar as a guest bartender. Live music runs close to seven nights a week, usually split into early and late shows, and Bluegrass Monday has become the signature night to catch. There's a fire pit and an outdoor stage out back, plus a front porch to grab some fresh air. The kitchen keeps it simple with Frito pie and BBQ sandwiches. It's a small room, so nobody's ever far from the stage.

venues.name: The Cobra
venues.shortDescription: East Nashville bar and venue known for punk, metal, indie, and late-night live shows. A raw, high-energy spot for catching heavier bands and underground music.

venues.name: Eastside Bowl
venues.shortDescription: East Nashville entertainment complex known for bowling, food, drinks, and touring shows at The '58. A go-to spot for concerts that pairs live music with a full night out.

venues.name: Riverside Revival
venues.shortDescription: East Nashville concert and event venue set inside a restored former church. An intimate space for live shows, special events, and performances with a more polished neighborhood feel.

venues.name: Music City Bar & Grill
venues.shortDescription: Music Valley country bar known for live music, late nights, and a mix of locals and visitors near Opryland. A casual spot for real country music without the Broadway crowds.

venues.name: Ray Stevens CabaRay Showroom
venues.shortDescription: West Nashville dinner theatre known for live music, comedy, and a classic showroom experience. Built around country entertainment, dinner, and old-school Nashville charm.
venues.whatToExpect: Ray Stevens CabaRay Showroom opened in West Nashville's Bellevue area in January 2018. Stevens built it as a Vegas-style dinner theater, its walls covered in Music Row session photos honoring Nashville classics like "Pretty Woman" and "El Paso," alongside memorabilia from his own career. For years, Stevens performed his own 90-minute show there, mixing comedy hits with stories from his career. That changed in March 2026, when the regular Thursday through Saturday show became Country Roads USA. It's an 11-person theatrical tribute written and directed by Dean Sams of Lonestar, tracing country music chronologically from 1928 to 2000 through artists like Hank Williams Sr. and Garth Brooks. The 75-minute show runs fast with no intermission, and it's family-friendly, with kids 12 and under getting in free. Though Stevens isn't performing nightly anymore, he still turns up for special one-off shows and guest appearances. Dinner comes before the show, with a Southern-style plated meal available on the main floor across three seating tiers by proximity to the stage (VIP, Elite, and Standard), or skip the meal for cheaper show-only seats in the balcony. The Bill Lowery High Spirits Emporium piano bar is named for the publisher who signed a 17-year-old Stevens as a songwriter in 1956. It opens before the show and stays open late after, with Tsunami Karaoke taking over Saturdays at 9pm. Parking is free.

venues.name: Night We Met
venues.shortDescription: Gulch nightclub and cocktail lounge centered around dance music, DJs, and late-night energy. A more elevated spot for electronic music and a different kind of Nashville nightlife.
venues.whatToExpect: Night We Met opened in March 2024 at 114 12th Avenue North in The Gulch, built specifically for house and electronic music in a city long dominated by country and rock. Mixmag, the international dance music outlet, called it Nashville's first nightclub built around electronic music, and the venue has said it's aiming to become one of the greenest clubs in the country. Founder Austin Knight also runs Full Circle Presents and co-founded the Deep Tropics music festival, giving him real standing in Nashville's dance music scene before the club even opened. Inside, the club splits into two rooms. The Vera Lounge opens first at 8pm, a more relaxed cocktail space before the night ramps up. The Moon Room takes over at 10pm, built around a Void Acoustics sound system that reviewers consistently single out for its clarity. Expect touring DJs and producers on any given weekend, alongside themed nights like 70s disco parties or tributes built around bands like Tame Impala. The club is open Thursday through Sunday, 21 and up, with a smart-casual dress code. Free parking is available at 1200 Broadway below the Whole Foods, with validation at the box office.
